newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Hollinger not close to Fairfax decision.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hollinger not close to Fairfax decision.

text.p: No decision is imminent on the fate of Conrad Black's stake in Australian newspaper group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, the president of Black's Hollinger Inc holding company said on Thursday.

David Radler said there was no panic to decide the future of the 25 percent stake. Company executives, including Black, have often said they would shed the holding if they were prevented by government rules from boosting it to 50 percent.
The Australian government said earlier today it would not widen its media industry review to include foreign ownership.
"I knew that four weeks ago," Radler said in a telephone interview.
On Wednesday, Black told reporters at the Fairfax annual meeting that he told Australia's prime minister that he wanted to raise the stake, held through Hollinger International, to 50 percent.
That would allow him to consolidate Fairfax's financial results under U.S. accounting rules.
Hollinger's newspaper interests include London's Daily and Sunday Telegraph, the Chicago Sun-Times, the Jerusalem Post, the Sydney Morning Herald and Southam Inc, Canada's biggest newspaper group.

Black said the Australian foreign media ownership rules, which bar foreign companies from holding more than 25 percent of newspaper groups and 15 percent of television companies, were "anachronistic".
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said earlier Thursday he currently saw no need to change the foreign media ownership limits.

Communications Minister Richard Alston said the government's current media review, originally designed to focus on cross-ownership restrictions, would not be broadened to include consideration of the foreign ownership rules.
"If it's not this inquiry, I think we'll have to wait and determine what's happening next. It's a very fluid situation -- it could change overnight," Radler said.
"We're not panicking, that's what I am telling you. We don't have to sell this thing tonight," he added.
Radler agreed that Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd would be a motivated buyer of any Fairfax holding if cross-media ownership restrictions were lifted by the inquiry.
Packer owns 15 percent of the group, while Rupert Murdoch owns five percent.

Packer, because of his Australian Nine Network, is also prevented by cross-media ownership from raising his stake. He has said he would like to merge his company with Fairfax if cross-media ownership rules were relaxed.
-- Sarah Edmonds, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100, E-mail sarah.edmonds@reuters.com
